english: Now eight candles stood in a row down the table. After their first dip the flames straightened, and they drew the whole long table into view, and in its center a yellow and purple dish of fruit. What had Rose done with it? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. For Rose’s arrangement—the grapes and pears, the horny shell lined with pink, the bananas—made her think of a trophy hauled up from the seabed, of a banquet of Neptune, of the cluster of grapes that hangs with its vine leaves over Bacchus’s shoulder (in some painting or other), among leopard skins and torches flaring and drooping, red and gold. … Lifted suddenly into the light like that, it seemed enormous and deep, like a world where you could pick up your walking stick and climb its hills, she thought, and walk down into its valleys. And to her delight (because for a moment it made them feel in tune) she saw that Augustus, too, was feasting his eyes on the same dish of fruit: diving in, snapping off a bloom here, a tassel there, and then, having feasted, going back to his hive. That was how he looked at things, not the way she did. But looking together brought them together.
danish_before_fix: Nu stod otte lys på række ned ad bordet. Efter deres første dyk rettede flammerne sig op, og de trak hele det lange bord frem i lyset, og midt på det et gult og purpurfarvet fad med frugt. Hvad havde Rose gjort ved det? undrede fru Ramsay sig. For Roses arrangement — druerne og pærerne, den hornede skal foret med pink, bananerne — fik hende til at tænke på et trofæ hevet op fra havbunden, på et gæstebud hos Neptun, på druekvasten, der hænger med sine vinblade over Bacchus skulder (i et eller andet maleri), blandt leopardskind og blussende, dryssende fakler i rødt og guld. … Hævet pludselig op i lyset på den måde virkede det enormt og dybt, som en verden, hvor man kunne tage sin stok og bestige dens bakker, tænkte hun, og gå ned i dens dale. Og til hendes glæde (for et øjeblik fik det dem til at føle sig i harmoni) så hun, at Augustus også gæstede det samme frugtfad med sine øjne: dykkede ned, nappede en blomst her, en dusk der, og så, efter at have gæstet, vendte tilbage til sin bikube. Sådan så han på tingene, ikke som hun gjorde. Men at se sammen bragte dem sammen.

english: Now all the candles were burning, and the candlelight drew the faces on either side of the table closer and gathered them, as the twilight had not, into a party sitting around a table. For now the night was shut out by panes of glass, and the glass, far from showing any true picture of the world outside, rippled it so oddly that in here, inside the room, there seemed to be order and solid ground, while out there was only a reflection in which things wavered and melted away, as if in water.
danish_before_fix: Nu brændte alle lysene, og levende lys trak ansigterne på begge sider af bordet tættere sammen og samlede dem, som tusmørket ikke havde gjort, til et selskab, der sad omkring et bord. For nu var natten lukket ude af rudeglas, og glasset, langt fra at vise noget sandt billede af verden udenfor, krusede den så mærkeligt, at herinde, inde i stuen, syntes at være orden og fast grund, mens derude kun var en genspejling, hvor ting vaklede og smeltede bort, som i vand.

english: “My grandmother’s recipe—it’s French,” said Mrs. Ramsay, and her voice rang with pleasure. French, naturally. What they call cooking in England is an abomination, the two of them agreed. It means dropping cabbages into water. It means roasting meat till it turns to leather. It means peeling away the lovely skins of vegetables. “And the skin,” Mr. Bankes put in, “is where all the virtue of the vegetable lies.” And then the waste, said Mrs. Ramsay. What an English cook throws out would feed an entire French family. She felt that William’s affection had returned to her, that all was well again, that the suspense was over and she was free now to triumph and to mock; and, spurred on by this, she laughed and waved her hands about, until Lily thought, How childlike she is, how absurd, sitting up there with all her beauty unfolded in her once more, talking about vegetable skins. There was something frightening in her. Nobody could resist her. In the end, Lily thought, she always had her way. Now she had managed this—Paul and Minta, it seemed, were engaged. Mr. Bankes was having dinner here. She cast a spell over all of them just by wanting things, so simply and so directly. Lily measured that abundance against her own poverty of spirit. Part of it, she supposed, was Mrs. Ramsay’s belief (her face was all lit up—she did not look young, but she looked radiant) in this strange and terrifying thing that had set Paul Rayley, at the center of it, trembling all over, and yet left him remote, absorbed and silent. As she talked about vegetable skins, Mrs. Ramsay, Lily felt, was exalting that thing, worshipping it, holding her hands over it both to warm them and to shelter it; and yet, having brought it all about, she was somehow laughing, leading her victims, Lily felt, to the altar. Now it came over Lily as well—the emotion, the vibration of love. Next to Paul, how unnoticeable she felt! He was glowing, burning; she was aloof and satirical. He was setting out on an adventure; she was moored to the shore. He was launched and heedless; she was alone, left out. And, ready to plead for a share in his disaster, if disaster it was, she asked shyly:
danish_before_fix: »Min bedstemors opskrift — den er fransk,« sagde fru Ramsay, og hendes stemme klang af fornøjelse. Fransk, naturligvis. Det, de kalder madlavning i England, er en vederstyggelighed, var de to enige om. Det betyder at smide kål i vand. Det betyder at stege kød, til det bliver til læder. Det betyder at skrælle de dejlige skind af grøntsagerne. »Og skindet,« kom hr. Bankes ind, »er der, hvor al grøntsagens dyd ligger.« Og så spildet, sagde fru Ramsay. Hvad en engelsk kokkepige smider ud, ville kunne brødføde en hel fransk familie. Hun følte, at Williams hengivenhed var vendt tilbage til hende, at alt var godt igen, at spændingen var forbi, og at hun nu var fri til at triumfere og håne; og, tilskyndet af dette, lo hun og viftede med hænderne, indtil Lily tænkte, Hvor barnlig hun er, hvor absurd, som hun sidder dér oppe med al sin skønhed udfoldet i sig igen og taler om grøntsagsskind. Der var noget skræmmende i hende. Ingen kunne modstå hende. Til sidst, tænkte Lily, fik hun altid sin vilje. Nu havde hun opnået dette — Paul og Minta var åbenbart forlovede. Hr. Bankes spiste middag her. Hun slog en trylleformular over dem alle blot ved at ville ting, så simpelt og så direkte. Lily målte den overflod mod sin egen åndelige fattigdom. En del af den, formodede hun, var fru Ramsays tro (hendes ansigt var helt oplyst — hun så ikke ung ud, men hun så strålende ud) på denne mærkelige og skræmmende ting, der havde fået Paul Rayley, midt i det hele, til at ryste over hele kroppen og alligevel gjort ham fjern, opslugt og tavs. Mens hun talte om grøntsagsskind, forherligede fru Ramsay, følte Lily, den ting, tilbad den, holdt sine hænder over den både for at varme dem og for at skærme den; og alligevel, efter at have bragt det hele i stand, lo hun på en eller anden måde og førte sine ofre, følte Lily, til alteret. Nu kom det også over Lily — følelsen, kærlighedens vibration. Ved siden af Paul, hvor ubemærket hun følte sig! Han glødede, brændte; hun var afstandtagende og satirisk. Han drog ud på et eventyr; hun lå fortøjet ved kysten. Han var sat i søen og ligeglad; hun var alene, udenfor. Og, parat til at bede om en andel i hans ulykke, om det så var en ulykke, spurgte hun sky:

english: That was how complicated things were. Because what happened to her, particularly when she stayed with the Ramsays, was that she was made to feel two contrary things, violently, both at once. One said, that’s what you feel; the other said, that’s what I feel; and then the two fought it out in her mind, as they were doing now. Love is so lovely, so thrilling, that I tremble on its brink and, quite unlike myself, volunteer to hunt for a brooch on a beach; and love is also the stupidest, most savage of human passions, and it takes a nice young man with a profile like a cameo (Paul’s profile was exquisite) and turns him into a bully with a crowbar (he was swaggering, he was insolent) in the Mile End Road, in the East End of London. And yet, she told herself, odes have been sung to love since the dawn of time, wreaths and roses have been piled up for it, and nine people out of ten, if you asked them, would say this was the one thing they wanted; while all along the women, to judge by her own experience, would be feeling, This isn’t what we want; nothing is more boring, more childish, more inhuman than love; and yet it is beautiful as well, and necessary. Well then? Well then? she asked, somehow expecting the others to take up the argument, as though in an argument of this kind you fired off your own small bolt, which obviously fell short, and left the rest to the others. So she listened once more to their talk, in case they shed some light on the question of love.
danish_before_fix: Sådan var tingene indviklede. For hvad der skete for hende, især når hun boede hos Ramsayerne, var, at hun blev fået til at føle to modsatte ting, voldsomt, begge på én gang. Den ene sagde, det er det, du føler; den anden sagde, det er det, jeg føler; og så kæmpede de to det ud i hendes sind, som de gjorde nu. Kærlighed er så dejlig, så spændende, at jeg skælver på dens rand og, helt ulig mig selv, melder mig til at lede efter en broche på en strand; og kærlighed er også den dummeste, mest vilde af menneskelige lidenskaber, og den tager en rar ung mand med en profil som en kamé (Pauls profil var udsøgt) og forvandler ham til en bølle med et brækjern (han strittede, han var uforskammet) i Mile End Road, i Londons East End. Og dog, sagde hun til sig selv, har man sunget oder til kærligheden siden tidernes morgen, kranse og roser er blevet hobet op for den, og ni mennesker ud af ti ville, hvis man spurgte dem, sige, at det var det eneste, de ønskede; mens kvinderne hele tiden, at dømme efter hendes egen erfaring, ville føle, Det er ikke det, vi vil have; intet er mere kedeligt, mere barnligt, mere umenneskeligt end kærlighed; og alligevel er den også smuk og nødvendig. Nå, så? Nå, så? spurgte hun, idet hun på en eller anden måde forventede, at de andre ville tage diskussionen op, som om man i en diskussion af denne slags afskød sin egen lille bolt, der åbenbart faldt til jorden, og overlod resten til de andre. Så hun lyttede endnu en gang til deres samtale, i tilfælde af at de kastede lys over spørgsmålet om kærlighed.

english: It had been foolish to seat them across from each other. That could be fixed tomorrow. If it was fine, they would go for a picnic. Anything seemed possible. Everything seemed right. Just now (though this can’t last, she thought, standing apart from the moment while the rest of them talked about boots), just now she had arrived at safety. She hovered like a hawk held still in the air; she floated like a flag in an element of joy that filled every nerve of her body, fully and sweetly—not loudly, but rather solemnly, because it came, she thought, as she watched them all eating, from her husband and children and friends. All this, rising in the deep stillness (she was giving William Bankes one very small piece more, and peering into the depths of the earthenware pot), now seemed, for no particular reason, to linger there like smoke, like a vapor drifting upward, keeping them safe together. Nothing needed saying; nothing could be said. There it was, all around them. It had something of eternity in it, she felt, as she carefully served Mr. Bankes an especially tender piece—just as she had felt once already that afternoon about something else. There is a coherence in things, a steadiness; something, she meant, that change cannot touch, and that shines out (she glanced at the window, rippling with reflected lights) against the flowing, the fleeting, the ghostly, like a ruby. So tonight, once more, she had the feeling she had had earlier today, of peace, of rest. It is from moments like these, she thought, that the thing is made that remains forever after. This would remain.
danish_before_fix: Det havde været tåbeligt at sætte dem overfor hinanden. Det kunne rettes i morgen. Hvis det var godt vejr, ville de tage på skovtur. Alt syntes muligt. Alt syntes rigtigt. Lige nu (skønt det ikke kan vare, tænkte hun, idet hun stod uden for øjeblikket, mens de andre talte om støvler), lige nu var hun nået frem til sikkerhed. Hun svævede som en høg, der holdes stille i luften; hun flød som et flag i et element af glæde, der fyldte hver nerve i hendes krop, fuldt og sødt — ikke højrøstet, men snarere højtideligt, for det kom, tænkte hun, mens hun så på dem alle, der spiste, fra hendes mand og børn og venner. Alt dette, der steg op i den dybe stilhed (hun gav William Bankes ét lille stykke mere og kiggede ned i den lerkrukkes dyb), syntes nu, uden nogen særlig grund, at blive hængende der som røg, som en damp, der drev opad og holdt dem trygt sammen. Intet behøvede at siges; intet kunne siges. Der var det, rundt om dem. Det havde noget af evighed i sig, følte hun, mens hun omhyggeligt serverede hr. Bankes et særlig mørt stykke — ligesom hun allerede en gang den eftermiddag havde følt om noget andet. Der er en sammenhæng i tingene, en stabilitet; noget, mente hun, som forandring ikke kan røre, og som skinner (hun kastede et blik på vinduet, der krusede af genspejlede lys) mod det flydende, det flygtige, det spøgelsesagtige, som en rubin. Så i aften havde hun endnu en gang den følelse, hun havde haft tidligere i dag, af fred, af hvile. Det er af øjeblikke som disse, tænkte hun, at den ting skabes, der forbliver for evigt efter. Dette ville forblive.

english: What did any of it mean? Even now she had no idea. A square root—what was that? Her sons knew. She leaned on them, on cubes and square roots, which was the subject now; on Voltaire and Madame de Staël; on Napoleon’s character; on how land was held in France; on Lord Rosebery; on Creevey’s Memoirs. She let this admirable structure of the masculine mind hold her up and carry her. It ran up and down and crisscrossed like iron girders across the swaying fabric, supporting the world, so that she could give herself up to it entirely, could even close her eyes, or let them flicker for a moment, the way a child lying on its pillow blinks up at the countless layers of leaves on a tree. Then she came to. The building was still going on. William Bankes was praising the Waverley novels.
danish_before_fix: Hvad betød det hele? Selv nu anede hun det ikke. En kvadratrod — hvad var det? Hendes sønner vidste det. Hun lænede sig op ad dem, op ad kuber og kvadratrødder, som var emnet nu; op ad Voltaire og Madame de Staël; op ad Napoleons karakter; op ad, hvordan jord blev besiddet i Frankrig; op ad Lord Rosebery; op ad Creeveys Erindringer. Hun lod denne beundringsværdige struktur af det maskuline sind holde hende oppe og bære hende. Den løb op og ned og på kryds og tværs som jernbjælker over den svajende væv, understøttende verden, så hun kunne give sig helt hen til den, endda lukke øjnene eller lade dem flakke et øjeblik, som et barn, der ligger på sin pude, blinker op mod de utallige lag af blade på et træ. Så kom hun til sig selv. Byggeriet var stadig i gang. William Bankes roste Waverley-romanerne.

english: All of a sudden she thought that she liked Charles Tansley; she liked the way he laughed. She liked him for being so angry with Paul and Minta. She liked his clumsiness. There was a good deal in that young man, after all. And Lily, she thought, laying her napkin beside her plate—Lily always has a private joke of her own. You never need to worry about Lily. She waited. She tucked her napkin under the rim of her plate. Well, had they finished now? No. One story had led to another. Her husband was in high spirits tonight; wanting, she supposed, to make up to old Augustus after that business over the soup, he had pulled him in, and the two of them were telling stories about someone they had both known at college. She looked at the window, where the candle flames burned brighter now that the panes had gone black, and as she gazed out there the voices reached her very strangely, like voices at a service in a cathedral, since she was not following the words. The sudden gusts of laughter, and then one voice (Minta’s) speaking by itself, reminded her of men and boys calling out the Latin of a service in some Roman Catholic cathedral. She waited. Her husband was speaking. He was repeating something, and she could tell it was poetry from the rhythm and from the note of exaltation and sadness in his voice:
danish_before_fix: Med ét tænkte hun, at hun kunne lide Charles Tansley; hun kunne lide den måde, han lo på. Hun kunne lide ham for at være så vred på Paul og Minta. Hun kunne lide hans kluntethed. Der var trods alt en hel del i den unge mand. Og Lily, tænkte hun, mens hun lagde sin serviet ved siden af sin tallerken — Lily har altid en privat spøg for sig selv. Man behøver aldrig bekymre sig om Lily. Hun ventede. Hun stak sin serviet ind under kanten af sin tallerken. Nå, var de færdige nu? Nej. Den ene historie havde ført til den anden. Hendes mand var i højt humør i aften; fordi han, formodede hun, ville råde bod på det over for gamle Augustus efter den affære med suppen, havde han trukket ham ind, og de to fortalte historier om nogen, de begge havde kendt på college. Hun så på vinduet, hvor lysets flammer brændte klarere nu, da ruderne var blevet sorte, og mens hun stirrede derud, nåede stemmerne hende så mærkeligt, som stemmer ved en gudstjeneste i en katedral, eftersom hun ikke fulgte ordene. De pludselige udbrud af latter, og så én stemme (Mintas), der talte for sig selv, mindede hende om mænd og drenge, der råbte latinen fra en gudstjeneste i en eller anden romersk-katolsk katedral. english: “All right, then,” said Mrs. Ramsay, “we’ll cover it up.” They all watched as she went to the chest of drawers and pulled open the little drawers one after another, fast; and when nothing in them would do, she whipped off her own shawl and wrapped it around the skull, round and round and round. Then she went back to Cam, laid her head almost flat on the pillow next to Cam’s, and told her how lovely it looked now; how the fairies would love it; it was like a bird’s nest; it was like a beautiful mountain of the kind she had seen abroad, with valleys and flowers and bells ringing and birds singing and little goats and antelopes. … As she said the words, rhythmically, she could see them echoing in Cam’s mind; Cam was saying after her that it was like a mountain, a bird’s nest, a garden, and there were little antelopes, and her eyes kept opening and closing. And Mrs. Ramsay kept on, ever more monotonous, ever more rhythmic and nonsensical, telling her to shut her eyes and sleep and dream of mountains and valleys and stars falling and parrots and antelopes and gardens and everything lovely, she said—lifting her head very slowly and speaking more and more mechanically—until she was sitting upright and could see that Cam had fallen asleep.
danish_before_fix: »Nå, men så,« sagde fru Ramsay, »dækker vi det til.« De så alle sammen på, mens hun gik hen til kommoden og hurtigt trak den ene lille skuffe ud efter den anden; og da intet i dem duede, rev hun sit eget sjal af og svøbte det om kraniet, rundt og rundt og rundt. Så gik hun tilbage til Cam, lagde sit hoved næsten fladt på puden ved siden af Cams og fortalte hende, hvor dejligt det så ud nu; hvor feerne ville elske det; det var som en fuglerede; det var som et smukt bjerg af den slags, hun havde set i udlandet, med dale og blomster og klokker, der ringede, og fugle, der sang, og små geder og antiloper. … Mens hun sagde ordene, rytmisk, kunne hun se dem give genlyd i Cams sind; Cam sagde dem efter hende, at det var som et bjerg, en fuglerede, en have, og at der var små antiloper, og hendes øjne gik hele tiden op og i. Og fru Ramsay blev ved, mere og mere enstonigt, mere og mere rytmisk og meningsløst, og bad hende lukke øjnene og sove og drømme om bjerge og dale og faldende stjerner og papegøjer og antiloper og haver og alt, hvad der var dejligt, sagde hun — mens hun løftede hovedet meget langsomt og talte mere og mere mekanisk — indtil hun sad opret og kunne se, at Cam var faldet i søvn.

english: Now, she whispered, going across to his bed, James had to go to sleep too, because look, she said, the boar’s skull was still there; nobody had touched it; they’d done exactly what he wanted; there it was, not hurt at all. He checked that the skull really was still under the shawl. But there was something else he wanted to ask her. Would they be going to the Lighthouse tomorrow?

Han tjekkede, at kraniet virkelig stadig var under sjalet. Men der var noget andet, han ville spørge hende om. Skulle de til Fyret i morgen?

english: She hoped he wouldn’t go banging his books on the floor above their heads, she thought, still dwelling on how irritating Charles Tansley was. Neither child was a good sleeper; they were excitable, and a man who could say such things about the Lighthouse seemed to her quite likely to knock over a pile of books just as they were dropping off, clumsily sweeping them off the table with his elbow. She assumed, that is, that he had gone up to work. And yet he looked so forlorn; and yet it would be a relief when he left; and yet she would see to it that he was treated better tomorrow; and yet he was wonderful with her husband; and yet his manners really did need improving; and yet she liked the way he laughed—and as she thought this, coming down the stairs, she noticed that the moon itself was now visible through the staircase window, the yellow harvest moon, and she turned; and they looked up and saw her standing above them on the stairs.
danish_before_fix: Hun håbede ikke, han ville gå og smække med sine bøger i gulvet over deres hoveder, tænkte hun, mens hun stadig dvælede ved, hvor irriterende Charles Tansley var. Ingen af børnene sov godt; de var ophidsede, og en mand, der kunne sige den slags om Fyret, forekom hende ganske i stand til at vælte en stak bøger lige som de var ved at dumme hen, ved klodset at feje dem af bordet med albuen. Hun gik, det vil sige, ud fra, at han var gået op for at arbejde. Og dog så han så forladt ud; og dog ville det være en lettelse, når han rejste; og dog ville hun sørge for, at han blev behandlet bedre i morgen; og dog var han vidunderlig over for hendes mand; og dog trængte hans manerer virkelig til at blive bedre; og dog kunne hun lide den måde, han lo på — og mens hun tænkte det, på vej ned ad trappen, lagde hun mærke til, at selve månen nu kunne ses gennem trappevinduet, den gule høstmåne, og hun vendte sig; og de så op og så hende stå over dem på trappen.

english: “That’s my mother,” Prue thought. Yes; Minta ought to look at her; Paul Rayley ought to look at her. There is the thing itself, she felt, as if there were only one such person in the whole world—her mother. A moment ago, chatting with the others, she had been completely grown-up; now she turned into a child again, and what they had been up to was a game, and she wondered whether her mother would allow their game or forbid it. And thinking what a chance this was for Minta and Paul and Lily to see her, and feeling what an amazing piece of luck it was that she herself had her, and that she would never grow up and never go away from home, she said, like a child, “We thought we’d go down to the beach and watch the waves.”
danish_before_fix: »Det er min mor,« tænkte Prue. Ja; Minta burde se på hende; Paul Rayley burde se på hende. Der er selve det, følte hun, som om der kun fandtes ét sådant menneske i hele verden — hendes mor. For et øjeblik siden, mens hun stod og snakkede med de andre, havde hun været fuldstændig voksen; nu blev hun til et barn igen, og det, de havde haft i sinde, var en leg, og hun spekulerede på, om hendes mor ville tillade deres leg eller forbyde den. Og mens hun tænkte på, hvilken chance det var for Minta og Paul og Lily at se hende, og følte, hvilken forbløffende heldig tilfældighed det var, at hun selv havde hende, og at hun aldrig ville blive voksen og aldrig forlade hjemmet, sagde hun, som et barn: »Vi tænkte, vi ville gå ned til stranden og se på bølgerne.«

english: “Yes, Paul does,” Minta said. Out of a small chamois-leather case Paul slid a beautiful gold watch to show her. And holding it out on his palm in front of her, he felt, “She knows everything. I don’t need to say a word.” What he was saying to her, as he showed her the watch, was, “I’ve done it, Mrs. Ramsay. I owe it all to you.” And looking at the gold watch lying in his hand, Mrs. Ramsay felt: What extraordinary luck Minta has! She’s marrying a man who keeps his gold watch in a chamois-leather bag!

english: Naturally, she told herself as she came in, she had had to come in here to fetch something she wanted. The first thing she wanted was to sit in one particular chair under one particular lamp. But she wanted something more besides, though what it was she did not know, could not think. Picking up her stocking and starting to knit, she glanced at her husband and saw that he did not want to be disturbed; that much was obvious. Whatever he was reading moved him deeply. He was half smiling, and then she could tell he was keeping his feelings under control. He was flipping the pages over. He was playing it out—maybe he fancied himself the man in the book. What book was it, she wondered. Oh, one of old Sir Walter Scott’s, she saw, tilting her lampshade so the light fell on her knitting. Because Charles Tansley had been saying (she looked up, half expecting to hear books crash to the floor overhead)—had been saying that nobody reads Scott any more. So her husband had thought, “That’s what they’ll say about me,” and had gone and fetched one of those books. And if he decided that Charles Tansley was right, he would accept it where Scott was concerned. (As he read she could see him weighing it up, considering, setting this against that.) But he would not accept it about himself. About himself he was always uneasy. That worried her. He would forever be fretting over his own books—will they be read, are they any good, why aren’t they better, what do people think of me? She didn’t like thinking of him that way; and wondering whether they had guessed at dinner why he turned so irritable all of a sudden when the talk was of fame and books that last, and whether the children were laughing about it, she gave the stocking a twitch; and around her lips and forehead all the fine lines appeared, as though cut with steel tools, and she grew still, like a tree that has been tossing and trembling and now, when the wind dies down, settles into quiet, one leaf after another.
danish_before_fix: Selvfølgelig, sagde hun til sig selv, mens hun kom ind, havde hun været nødt til at komme herind for at hente noget, hun ville have. Det første, hun ville, var at sidde i en bestemt stol under en bestemt lampe. Men hun ville noget mere, selv om hvad det var, vidste hun ikke, kunne ikke tænke sig til. Hun tog sin strømpe op og begyndte at strikke, kastede et blik på sin mand og så, at han ikke ville forstyrres; så meget var tydeligt. Hvad han end læste, rørte det ham dybt. Han smilede halvt, og så kunne hun mærke, at han holdt sine følelser nede. Han bladrede siderne om. Han spillede det igennem — måske forestillede han sig, at han var manden i bogen. Hvilken bog var det, undrede hun sig. Åh, en af gamle Sir Walter Scotts, så hun, mens hun vippede lampeskærmen, så lyset faldt på hendes strikketøj. For Charles Tansley havde sagt (hun så op, halvt i forventning om at høre bøger styrte i gulvet ovenover) — havde sagt, at ingen læste Scott mere. Så hendes mand havde tænkt: »Sådan vil de sige om mig,« og var gået hen og havde hentet en af de bøger. Og hvis han besluttede, at Charles Tansley havde ret, ville han acceptere det, hvad Scott angik. (Mens han læste, kunne hun se ham veje det, overveje det, sætte det ene op mod det andet.) Men han ville ikke acceptere det om sig selv. Om sig selv var han altid urolig. Det bekymrede hende. Han ville evigt gå og græmmes over sine egne bøger — vil de blive læst, er de gode, hvorfor er de ikke bedre, hvad tænker folk om mig? Hun brød sig ikke om at tænke på ham på den måde; og mens hun spekulerede på, om de havde gættet ved middagen, hvorfor han pludselig var blevet så irritabel, da talen faldt på berømmelse og bøger, der består, og om børnene grinede af det, gav hun strømpen et ryk; og rundt om hendes læber og pande kom alle de fine linjer til syne, som skåret med stålredskaber, og hun blev stille, som et træ, der har knejset og dirret og nu, da vinden lægger sig, falder til ro, det ene blad efter det andet.

english: None of it mattered, she thought. A great man, a great book, fame—who could say? She knew nothing about such things. But it was just his way, his honesty—at dinner, for example, she had caught herself thinking, quite by instinct, If only he would speak! She trusted him entirely. And letting all this go by, the way a diver slips past first a weed, then a straw, then a bubble, she felt again, sinking lower, what she had felt in the hall while the others talked: There is something I want—something I came here for. And, eyes shut, she sank further and further down, not quite knowing what it was. For a while she waited, knitting, wondering; and gradually the words they had said at dinner, “the China rose is all abloom and buzzing with the honey bee,” started washing to and fro across her mind in rhythm. And as they washed back and forth, words like small shaded lamps—a red one, a blue one, a yellow one—lit up in her mind’s darkness and seemed to leave their high perches and fly across and back again, or to call out and be answered by echoes. So she turned and felt around on the table next to her for a book.
danish_before_fix: Intet af det betød noget, tænkte hun. En stor mand, en stor bog, berømmelse — hvem kunne sige det? Hun vidste intet om den slags. Men det var bare hans måde, hans ærlighed — ved middagen, for eksempel, havde hun grebet sig selv i at tænke, ganske instinktivt: Bare han ville sige noget! Hun stolede fuldstændigt på ham. Og mens hun lod alt dette glide forbi, som en dykker glider forbi først et ukrudt, så et strå, så en boble, mærkede hun igen, mens hun sank dybere, det, hun havde mærket i hallen, mens de andre talte: Der er noget, jeg vil have — noget, jeg kom herind for. Og med lukkede øjne sank hun længere og længere ned, uden helt at vide, hvad det var. I et stykke tid ventede hun, strikkende, og undrede sig; og efterhånden begyndte de ord, de havde sagt ved middagen, »den kinesiske rose står i fuldt flor og summer af honningbien«, at skylle frem og tilbage over hendes sind i takt. Og mens de skyllede frem og tilbage, tændtes ord som små skærmede lamper — en rød, en blå, en gul — i hendes sinds mørke og syntes at forlade deres høje pladser og flyve over og tilbage igen, eller at kalde og få svar af ekkoer. Så hun vendte sig og famlede på bordet ved siden af sig efter en bog.

english: Well, let them do better than that, he thought, finishing the chapter. He had the feeling of having argued with someone and won. Whatever they said, they could not do better than that; and his own standing felt more secure. The lovers were rubbish, he thought, gathering the whole thing together in his mind once more. That part’s rubbish, this part’s first-rate, he thought, setting one piece against another. But he would have to read it again. The overall shape of it escaped him. He must keep his verdict open. So he went back to his other thought—if the young men didn’t care for this, then of course they didn’t care for him either. You mustn’t complain, Mr. Ramsay told himself, trying to smother his wish to complain to his wife that the young men didn’t admire him. But he had made up his mind: he would not bother her again. At this point he looked over at her, reading. She looked very peaceful as she read. He liked to think that the others had all gone off and left the two of them alone. Going to bed with a woman was not the whole of life, he thought, turning back to Scott and Balzac, to the English novel and the French.
danish_before_fix: Nå, lad dem gøre det bedre end det, tænkte han, mens han færdiggjorde kapitlet. Han havde en følelse af at have skændtes med nogen og vundet. Hvad de end sagde, kunne de ikke gøre det bedre end det; og hans egen stilling føltes mere sikker. De forelskede var noget makværk, tænkte han, mens han endnu en gang samlede det hele i sit sind. Den del er makværk, den del er førsteklasses, tænkte han og stillede det ene stykke op mod det andet. Men han måtte læse det igen. Den overordnede form undslap ham. Han måtte holde sin dom åben. Så han vendte tilbage til sin anden tanke — hvis de unge mænd ikke brød sig om dette, så brød de selvfølgelig heller ikke om ham. Man må ikke klage, sagde hr. Ramsay til sig selv og forsøgte at kvæle sit ønske om at klage over for sin kone over, at de unge mænd ikke beundrede ham. Men han havde besluttet sig: han ville ikke plage hende igen. Her så han over på hende, der læste. Hun så meget fredfyldt ud, mens hun læste. Han syntes om at tænke, at de andre alle var gået og havde ladet de to alene. At gå i seng med en kvinde var ikke hele livet, tænkte han og vendte sig tilbage til Scott og Balzac, til den engelske roman og den franske.

english: He said nothing, but swung the compass on his watch-chain to and fro, thinking about Scott’s novels and Balzac’s. Yet through the dusky walls of their closeness—for they were drawing together without meaning to, coming side by side, very near—she could feel his mind like a hand lifted over hers, throwing it into shade. And now that her thoughts were turning in a direction he disliked, toward what he called her “pessimism,” he began to fidget, though he still did not speak—putting a hand to his forehead, twisting a strand of hair, letting it drop.
danish_before_fix: Han sagde intet, men svingede kompasset på sin urkæde frem og tilbage og tænkte på Scotts romaner og Balzacs. Og dog kunne hun gennem deres nærheds skumrende vægge — for de nærmede sig hinanden uden at mene det, kom side om side, helt tæt — mærke hans sind som en hånd, løftet over hendes, der kastede den i skygge. Og nu, da hendes tanker drejede i en retning, han ikke brød sig om, mod det, han kaldte hendes »pessimisme«, begyndte han at rumstere, selv om han stadig ikke talte — han førte en hånd til panden, snoede en hårtot og lod den falde.

english: “You won’t get that stocking finished tonight,” he said, pointing at it. That was just what she wanted—the edge in his voice as he scolded her. If he says being pessimistic is wrong, then it’s probably wrong, she thought; the marriage will turn out fine.

english: And then what? She could feel that he was still looking at her, but that the look was different now. He wanted something—the thing she always found so hard to give him: he wanted her to say that she loved him. And that, no, she could not do. Talking came so much more easily to him than to her. He was able to say things—she never was. So of course it was always he who said them; and then, for some reason, he would suddenly resent it and reproach her. A heartless woman, he called her; she never once told him she loved him. But that wasn’t true—it wasn’t true. It was only that she never could put what she felt into words. Wasn’t there a crumb on his coat? Nothing she could do for him? She got up and stood at the window holding the reddish-brown stocking, partly to turn away from him and partly because now, with him watching, she did not mind looking at the Lighthouse. For she knew he had turned his head when she turned; he was watching her. She knew what he was thinking: You are more beautiful than ever. And she felt very beautiful. Won’t you tell me just this once that you love me? That was what he was thinking, because he was stirred—what with Minta, and his book, and the day coming to an end, and their quarrel about going to the Lighthouse. But she couldn’t; she couldn’t say it. Then, knowing he was watching her, instead of speaking she turned around, the stocking in her hands, and looked at him. And as she looked at him she began to smile, for although she had not said a word, he knew—of course he knew—that she loved him. He could not deny it. And smiling, she looked out of the window and said (thinking to herself, Nothing on earth can equal this happiness)—
danish_before_fix: Og hvad så? Hun kunne mærke, at han stadig så på hende, men at blikket var anderledes nu. Han ville have noget — det, hun altid fandt så svært at give ham: han ville have, at hun skulle sige, at hun elskede ham. Og det, nej, det kunne hun ikke. Det at tale faldt ham så meget lettere end hende. Han var i stand til at sige tingene — det var hun aldrig. Så naturligvis var det altid ham, der sagde dem; og så ville han af en eller anden grund pludselig tage det ilde op og bebrejde hende. En hjerteløs kvinde, kaldte han hende; hun fortalte ham aldrig, at hun elskede ham. Men det var ikke sandt — det var ikke sandt. Det var bare, at hun aldrig kunne sætte ord på det, hun følte. Var der ikke en krumme på hans jakke? Intet, hun kunne gøre for ham? Hun rejste sig og stillede sig ved vinduet med den rødbrune strømpe i hånden, dels for at vende sig bort fra ham og dels fordi hun nu, mens han så på hende, ikke havde noget imod at se på Fyret. For hun vidste, at han havde drejet hovedet, da hun vendte sig; han betragtede hende. Hun vidste, hvad han tænkte: Du er smukkere end nogensinde. Og hun følte sig meget smuk. Vil du ikke sige mig bare denne ene gang, at du elsker mig? Det var, hvad han tænkte, for han var bevæget — på grund af Minta, og sin bog, og dagen, der gik på hæld, og deres skænderi om at tage til Fyret. Men hun kunne ikke; hun kunne ikke sige det. Så, i vished om at han betragtede hende, vendte hun sig i stedet for at tale om, med strømpen i hænderne, og så på ham. Og mens hun så på ham, begyndte hun at smile, for selv om hun ikke havde sagt et ord, vidste han — selvfølgelig vidste han — at hun elskede ham. Det kunne han ikke benægte. Og smilende så hun ud ad vinduet og sagde (mens hun tænkte ved sig selv: Intet på jorden kan måle sig med denne lykke) —

english: But what, after all, is one night? A short space of time, especially when the darkness fades so soon, and so soon a bird sings, a cock crows, or a faint green stirs, like a turning leaf, in the hollow of the wave. Night, however, follows night. Winter holds a whole pack of them in reserve and deals them out equally, evenly, with tireless fingers. They lengthen; they darken. Some of them hold up clear planets, plates of brightness. The autumn trees, ravaged as they are, take on the gleam of tattered flags glowing in the gloom of cool cathedral vaults, where gold letters on marble pages describe death in battle, and bones bleaching and burning far away in Indian sands. The autumn trees shine in the yellow moonlight, in the light of harvest moons—the light that softens the energy of labor, and smooths the stubble, and brings the wave lapping blue to the shore.
danish_before_fix: Men hvad er egentlig én nat? Et kort stykke tid, især når mørket så hurtigt svinder, og så snart en fugl synger, en hane galer, eller noget svagt grønt rører sig som et vendende blad i bølgens fordybning. Men nat følger på nat. Vinteren har en hel bunke af dem i reserve og deler dem ud lige og jævnt med utrættelige fingre. De bliver længere; de bliver mørkere. Nogle af dem holder klare planeter op, skiver af lys. Efterårets træer, hærgede som de er, får glansen fra laset faner, der gløder i de kølige katedralhvælvingers dunkel, hvor guldbogstaver på marmorsider beskriver døden i kamp og knogler, der blegner og brænder langt borte i Indiens sand. Efterårets træer skinner i det gule måneskin, i høstmånernes lys — det lys, der dæmper arbejdets energi og glatter stubbene og får bølgen til at skvulpe blå mod stranden.

english: The nights now are full of wind and destruction. The trees plunge and bend, and their leaves fly helter-skelter until the lawn is plastered with them and they lie packed in gutters, choke the rain-pipes and litter the damp paths. The sea, too, tosses itself and breaks itself; and if some sleeper, imagining that he might find on the beach an answer to his doubts, someone to share his solitude, should throw off his bedclothes and go down alone to walk on the sand, no image that seems to serve him with divine readiness comes easily to hand, bringing the night to order and making the world reflect the range of the soul. The hand dwindles in his hand; the voice bellows in his ear. It would almost seem useless, in such confusion, to ask the night those questions—what, and why, and for what purpose—that tempt the sleeper from his bed to look for an answer.
danish_before_fix: Nætterne er nu fulde af vind og ødelæggelse. Træerne styrter og bøjer sig, og bladene flyver hulter til bulter, til plænen er klistret til med dem, og de ligger stuvet sammen i render, tilstopper nedløbsrørene og dækker de fugtige stier. Havet kaster sig også omkring og brækker sig selv; og hvis en søvnløs, der forestillede sig, at han på stranden kunne finde svar på sine tvivl, en at dele sin ensomhed med, skulle kaste dynen af sig og gå alene ned for at gå på sandet, så byder intet billede sig let, som med guddommelig beredvillighed vil tjene ham, bringe natten i orden og få verden til at spejle sjælens vidde. Hånden svinder ind i hans hånd; stemmen brøler i hans øre. Det synes næsten nytteløst i en sådan forvirring at stille natten de spørgsmål — hvad, og hvorfor, og til hvilket formål — som lokker den søvnløse ud af sengen for at søge et svar.
